title: Contraceptives
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Contraception and Pharmacological Principles
headings.content: Contraception encompasses methods and devices used to prevent pregnancy by interfering with the normal processes of ovulation, fertilization, and implantation. Pharmacologically, agents rely on mimicking endogenous sex hormones, creating physical barriers, or altering the intrauterine environment to inhibit gamete viability or transport. Understanding the **Pearl Index** is fundamental for evaluating contraceptive efficacy, representing the number of unintended pregnancies occurring per 100 women-years of exposure. Methods vary widely in typical use versus perfect use, reflecting human behavioral factors such as adherence and consistency. In Nigerian clinical practice, appreciating these pharmacological foundations allows nurses to provide realistic success rates during family planning consultations, moving beyond theoretical laboratory perfection to practical real-world efficacy.

headings.title: Hormonal Contraceptives: Mechanisms and Classifications
headings.content:
Hormonal contraceptives primarily utilize synthetic estrogens and progestins to manipulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. The three core mechanisms of action include:

- **Inhibition of Ovulation**: Exogenous hormones provide negative feedback to the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, suppressing the mid-cycle surge of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone.
- **Cervical Mucus Thickening**: Progestins induce the secretion of scanty, viscous cervical mucus that physically blocks sperm penetration into the upper reproductive tract.
- **Endometrial Alteration**: Continuous hormone exposure causes endometrial atrophy, rendering the uterine lining hostile and non-receptive to blastocyst implantation.

Classifications span combination products containing both estrogen and progestin derivatives, as well as progestin-only formulations administered via various systemic routes.

headings.title: Combined Oral Contraceptives and Injectable Formulations
headings.content: Combined Oral Contraceptives typically combine ethinyl estradiol with a synthetic progestin such as levonorgestrel or drospirenone, packaged in 21-day or 28-day regimens. The hormone-free interval in 28-day packs induces a scheduled withdrawal bleed. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is an injectable progestin administered intramuscularly or subcutaneously every three months, offering discrete and highly effective systemic coverage. Pharmacokinetically, injectables provide a sustained-release depot effect, avoiding first-pass hepatic metabolism immediately after absorption. In busy Nigerian primary health clinics, injectables remain highly favored due to their discretion and infrequent administration schedule, though clients must receive clear counseling regarding potential return-to-fertility delays.

headings.title: Progestin-Only Options and Emergency Contraception
headings.content: Progestin-only pills, often called the mini-pill, must be taken at the exact same time every day due to their short half-life and reliance on cervical mucus changes rather than consistent ovulation suppression. Emergency contraceptive pills contain high doses of levonorgestrel or selective progesterone receptor modulators like ulipristal acetate. They operate by delaying or inhibiting ovulation if taken before the luteinizing hormone surge begins. They do not disrupt an established pregnancy or implant embryo, functioning purely as pre-fertilization blockers. Pharmacists and nurses in emergency settings must emphasize that emergency pills are intended for acute unprotected episodes and should not substitute for regular ongoing birth control methods.

headings.title: Long-Acting Reversible Contraception and Barrier Methods
headings.content: Long-acting reversible contraception includes intrauterine devices and subdermal progestin implants. Intrauterine devices are categorized into copper-bearing devices, which release copper ions toxic to sperm and ova, and hormone-releasing intrauterine systems that locally suppress the endometrium. Subdermal implants slowly release progestin over three to five years, boasting failure rates of less than one percent. Barrier methods—such as male and female condoms, diaphragms, and cervical caps—provide physical blocks against gamete encounter while uniquely offering dual protection against sexually transmitted infections. Combining barrier methods with hormonal agents maximizes both infection prevention and pregnancy avoidance.

headings.title: Pharmacological Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
headings.content: Estrogen excess can manifest as breast tenderness, fluid retention, nausea, and headaches. Conversely, estrogen deficiency may cause breakthrough bleeding, vasomotor symptoms, and atrophic vaginitis. Progestin excess contributes to weight gain, acne, hirsutism, and mood changes. The most serious adverse reaction associated with estrogen-containing formulations is venous thromboembolism, driven by hepatic stimulation of clotting factors. Nurses must remain vigilant for the classic signs of thromboembolic events, encapsulated by the acronym ACHES: Abdominal pain, Chest pain, Headaches, Eye problems, and Severe leg pain.

headings.title: Contraindications and Drug Interactions
headings.content: Safety screening is paramount before prescribing hormonal agents. Combined methods are strictly contraindicated in women with a history of deep vein thrombosis, ischemic heart disease, severe hypertension, complicated valvular heart disease, or migraines with aura due to stroke risks. Smokers over the age of 35 face significantly elevated cardiovascular risks when taking estrogen. Furthermore, hepatic enzyme-inducing medications—such as certain anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin) and antitubercular drugs (rifampicin)—accelerate the metabolism of contraceptive steroids, drastically reducing their pharmacological efficacy and requiring alternative non-hormonal backups.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment, Patient Education, and Counseling in Nigeria
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care requires taking a thorough medical, gynecological, and social history to match the client with the safest and most effective method. In many Nigerian communities, cultural beliefs, partner dynamics, and social stigma surrounding premarital sex or family planning can hinder open communication. Nurses must offer confidential, non-judgmental counseling, addressing common myths such as permanent sterility caused by injectables or implants. Education should cover correct usage, missed dose protocols, expected side effects, and warning signs requiring immediate medical re-evaluation, empowering clients to make informed reproductive health choices.
